input.instructions: Create a compact, accurate blueprint for an 8-to-12-minute educational lesson with exactly ten sequential teaching beats. Do not write full narration. Create exactly three measurable learning objectives. For every beat, provide one distinct complete factual claim, a concrete example, a concise editable visual direction, and one or two exact supplied source IDs. End the claim, example, and visual direction with complete punctuation. Every cited source excerpt must directly support the claim; reuse at least two important technical terms from each cited excerpt so support can be checked locally. Do not invent course assignments, policies, measurements, datasets, instruction encodings, or product behavior that is absent from the supplied excerpts. Keep the claim, example, and visual direction compact; a deterministic local expander will produce the full narration. Sequence the beats from foundations through application and end with a practical analysis checklist. Use only the supplied source excerpts for factual claims. Every factual claim must cite one or more supplied source IDs. Narration must describe information that is essential to understand visuals. Do not imitate a named creator or invent sources.

Topic: CSCI-605: Advanced Object-Oriented Programming Concepts. Create a representative course-foundations companion aligned to the official catalog description. It must teach durable concepts and problem-solving methods without claiming to replace the instructor's syllabus. Official catalog description: This course focuses on identifying advanced object-oriented programming concepts and implementing them in the context of specific problems. This course covers advanced concepts such as event-driven programming, design patterns, distributed and concurrent programming, and the use, design and implementation of applications. Assignments (both in class and as homework) requiring a solution to a problem and an implementation in code are an integral part of the course. Note: This course serves as a bridge course for graduate students and cannot be taken by undergraduate students without permission from the CS Undergraduate Program Coordinator. This course is restricted to students in COMPSCI-MS. Contact Hours: Lecture 3 Typically Offered: Fall, Spring

Source excerpts:

[nist-cloud]
NIST defines cloud computing with five essential characteristics. On-demand self-service allows consumers to provision capabilities without requiring human interaction with each provider. Broad network access makes capabilities available over networks through standard mechanisms. Resource pooling serves multiple consumers with dynamically assigned physical and virtual resources. Rapid elasticity allows capabilities to scale outward and inward according to demand. Measured service monitors and reports resource use. NIST identifies software, platform, and infrastructure service models. NIST also identifies private, community, public, and hybrid deployment models. Sound cloud analysis makes trust boundaries, tenancy, failure domains, scaling assumptions, observability, and responsibility allocation explicit.

[raft-paper]
Raft decomposes consensus into leader election, log replication, and safety. Servers move among follower, candidate, and leader states. Terms act as logical clocks and allow servers to identify stale information. A follower starts an election after its election timeout elapses without valid leader communication. A candidate requests votes and becomes leader after receiving votes from a majority. A leader appends client commands to its log and sends entries to followers. An entry becomes committed after the required majority condition is satisfied. Log matching and election restrictions preserve the safety properties described by the algorithm.

[rit-csci-605]
This course focuses on identifying advanced object-oriented programming concepts and implementing them in the context of specific problems. This course covers advanced concepts such as event-driven programming, design patterns, distributed and concurrent programming, and the use, design and implementation of applications. Assignments (both in class and as homework) requiring a solution to a problem and an implementation in code are an integral part of the course. Note: This course serves as a bridge course for graduate students and cannot be taken by undergraduate students without permission from the CS Undergraduate Program Coordinator. This course is restricted to students in COMPSCI-MS. Contact Hours: Lecture 3 Typically Offered: Fall, Spring
